text: Every request and response body in chapter one was JSON. It won out over older formats because it's compact, maps directly onto the dictionaries and lists almost every language already has, and a human can read it without any extra tooling.

JSON supports exactly six types, no more. Strings, always in double quotes. Numbers, no quotes. Booleans — true or false. Null, meaning explicitly nothing. Objects, for key-value pairs. Arrays, for ordered lists. If you need a date, you send a string and agree on a format.

Here's valid JSON, start to finish. Keys are always strings in double quotes — never single quotes, never bare. Every pair gets a comma, except the last one — that one must not have a trailing comma. Objects use curly braces, arrays use square brackets.

Two containers, two different jobs. An object is unordered — you look things up by name. An array is ordered — you look things up by position. Getting that distinction right matters the moment you start parsing real responses, in lesson nine.
Six types, strict punctuation, two container shapes. Next lesson, we go one level deeper: JSON nested inside JSON, which is what every real API response actually looks like.
